title: Tuning a servo
summary: From a motor's time constant to a position servo: proportional gain and overshoot, derivative damping, an integral against a load, and windup at the supply limit.

steps.title: The motor's time constant
steps.text:
Apply a 12 V step to the motor alone. The back-EMF K ω grows with the speed and eats into the voltage, so the speed rises like a first-order system and levels off at K V / (K² + b R).

The time constant is τ = J R / (K² + b R): about 0.2 s for this motor. Run it and read Time to 63 % in the Summary (the armature inductance adds a few milliseconds).

check.success: τ ≈ 0.2 s, and about 1120 rpm at 12 V. The Poles tab shows the same thing as a pole at −1/τ ≈ −5.2 per second, with the electrical pole far to the left at about −395.

steps.title: Position control: proportional gain
steps.text:
Now close the loop on the angle: V = Kp (θ_ref − θ), here with Kp = 5 V/rad and a 90° step. The motor's own damping is weak, so the closed loop is a lightly damped second-order system.

Run it and watch the Animation: the pointer swings past the reference and rings. The Poles tab shows the closed-loop pair and its damping ratio ζ.

check.success: About 65 % overshoot. The closed-loop pair has ζ ≈ 0.14, for which e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) predicts 64 %; the fast electrical pole adds a little. Raising Kp makes it faster but even less damped.

steps.title: Add derivative
steps.text:
A derivative term, −Kd ω, brakes the motor in proportion to its speed. It adds damping without changing ω_n: 2 ζ ω_n = (K²/R + b + K Kd / R) / J.

Set Kd so the overshoot falls below 5 % (Kd = 0.4 V·s/rad gives ζ ≈ 0.8) and run.

check.success: Well damped, and settled in a fraction of the time. The PD preset raises Kp to 10 as well, for a faster response.

steps.title: A load needs an integral
steps.text:
Hang a 0.1 N·m load on the shaft at 0.2 s while the PD servo holds 0°. To carry the load the motor needs a current τ / K, so a voltage, and a PD controller only makes a voltage from an error: it settles with θ off by τ R / (K Kp) ≈ 11.5°.

Run it and see the error in the Error and power tab. Then add an integral (Ki = 50 V/(rad·s)) and run again.

check.success: The integral keeps growing until the error is gone: it ends up holding exactly the voltage the load needs.

steps.title: Saturation and windup
steps.text:
Ask the PID servo for a full turn with only 12 V. The command saturates for about 0.14 s, and all that time the integral keeps adding up the large error: it winds up, and has to unwind past the target. Run it: almost 50 % overshoot.

Switch Anti-windup to Clamping, which holds the integral while the voltage is saturated and the error would push it further, and run again.

check.hint: Choose Clamping under Anti-windup and run.
check.success: About 13 % instead of 49 %. Tick Keep previous runs and compare the two in the Angle and speed tab: same gains, same motor, only the integral's behaviour while saturated differs.
